personas.name: Refund-Runway Rae (Aid-Dependent, Lump-Sum Disbursement)
personas.demographic: 18-24, US undergraduate at a public 4-year or community college, Pell-eligible (household income typically <$60K), often first-generation. Part-time wage income plus 1-2 lump-sum aid refunds per term.
personas.psychographic: Anxiety-driven relationship with money; feast-or-famine mindset. Money is a top stressor tied to persistence. Wants control but lacks a mental model for pacing a big deposit over ~4 months.
personas.behavioral: Receives one large refund at term start, spends fastest weeks 1-4, runs short by mid-term. Uses free tools (bank app, spreadsheet). MDRC 'Aid Like a Paycheck' RCT (~9,000 students) confirms the lump-sum-to-shortfall pattern.
painPoints: No tool converts lump-sum refund into per-week/per-month term runway
Runs out of money before next disbursement
Irregular income breaks fixed-budget apps built for salaried adults
personas.willingnessToPay: LOW absolute WTP but real: most budget-constrained persona (Pell = need-based). YNAB gives students a FREE year, signaling category treats students as free/low-margin. Monetization more likely via B2B2C (colleges, MDRC-style programs) than direct consumer subscriptions.

personas.name: First-Budget Finn (First-Time Money Manager)
personas.demographic: 18-20, traditional-age undergraduate, broad income range, first time managing own money away from parents.
personas.psychographic: No budgeting habit yet; learns via app/social (TikTok finance), values simplicity and automation over spreadsheets. Open to 'AI does it for me' framing.
personas.behavioral: Adopts free apps readily; churns quickly with friction. Overlaps with subscription-heavy behavior.
painPoints: Doesn't know how to start a budget or what 'normal' spending is
Existing apps assume prior financial literacy
personas.willingnessToPay: LOW-to-MODERATE. High free-app adoption, low paid conversion; but pays for OTHER app categories (~$97/mo media/subscriptions per Talker Research). WTP exists but is spent on entertainment, not finance.

personas.name: Splitwise Sam (Cost-Sharing Roommate/Friend Group)
personas.demographic: 19-23, lives off-campus or shared housing, splits rent/utilities/groceries/subscriptions with 2-5 people.
personas.psychographic: Socially motivated; wants to avoid awkward money conversations. Trusts a bill-splitting app but sees it as siloed from personal budgeting.
personas.behavioral: Active Splitwise/Venmo user. Splitwise reports 35M+ global users; ~38% of Gen Z regularly use digital expense-sharing tools. Bill-splitting apps market ~$612M in 2025, ~7-8% CAGR.
painPoints: Shared costs live in Splitwise; personal budget lives elsewhere — no unified view
Group subscriptions and rent create recurring reconciliation overhead
personas.willingnessToPay: MODERATE — strongest paid signal of the five. A paid bill-splitting market already exists (Splitwise Pro monetizes), proving this cohort will pay for shared-cost tooling.

personas.name: Subscription-Stack Sky (Subscription-Heavy Gen Z Spender)
personas.psychographic: Convenience-first, prone to subscription creep and set-and-forget billing; motivated by 'save money / cancel waste' hooks.
personas.behavioral: Holds ~8+ subscriptions; 35% pay for unwanted ones. Subscribes to ~26% more services than average American (Bango); spends ~$97/mo on media (Talker Research).
painPoints: No single place tracks recurring drains against income
personas.willingnessToPay: MODERATE-to-HIGH relative to peers. Clearest 'save-me-money' ROI story and proven discretionary spend.

personas.name: Currency-Crossing Camila (International Student)
personas.demographic: 18-24, F-1 undergraduate; 357,231 international undergrads in US 2024/25 (IIE Open Doors). Top origins India, China.
personas.psychographic: Managing money across two currencies and cultures; risk-averse about fees; no US credit history yet.
personas.behavioral: Tracks forex, remittances, multi-currency balances; underserved by US-centric budgeting apps.
painPoints: Multi-currency budgeting and forex fee tracking
No US credit history — excluded from credit-linked features
US apps assume single-currency, domestic-banking user
personas.willingnessToPay: MODERATE. Smaller segment but higher relative spend capacity (often self-funded) and acute unmet need.

primaryAudience.segment: Aid-dependent US undergraduates receiving lump-sum financial-aid refunds, overlapping with first-time money managers
primaryAudience.estimatedSize: ~5.8M-6.0M core (Pell recipients as proxy): 6,032,974 in AY2022-23, 6.3-6.5M AY2023-24 (Federal Student Aid / educationdata.org). Broader ceiling: ~19.28M undergrads (Fall 2024, NCES) x 72% receiving some aid ≈ 13.9M, or x 55% federal aid ≈ 10.6M.
primaryAudience.rationale: Highest severity in upstream problem discovery, largest well-bounded population, institutionally validated pain (MDRC RCT). Only segment where pacing a lump sum into a term runway has no incumbent. Trade-off: lowest-WTP segment (need-based by definition) — monetization likely requires B2B2C/institutional or freemium rather than direct consumer subscriptions.

secondaryAudiences.estimatedSize: Overlaps most of ~19.28M undergrads; ~8+ subs each, 35% carry unwanted subs

secondaryAudiences.segment: Cost-sharing roommates/friend groups (strongest existing paid-market proof)
secondaryAudiences.estimatedSize: ~38% of Gen Z regularly use expense-sharing apps; bill-splitting market ~$612M in 2025

secondaryAudiences.segment: International undergraduates (high per-user need, smaller base)

icp.description: A US undergraduate (18-22) who receives a lump-sum financial-aid refund each term AND earns irregular part-time wages, is a first-time money manager, and already pays for consumer subscriptions (proving WTP exists) — giving both acute lump-sum-runway pain and a 'save-me-money-on-subscriptions' monetization hook. Reachable via campus financial-aid offices and first-year onboarding.
criteria: Enrolled undergraduate, age 18-22, in the US
Pell-eligible / receives lump-sum aid refund at least once per term
Has part-time wage income (irregular cash flow)
Reachable via financial-aid office, first-year seminars, or campus partnerships

sources.description: NCES / educationdata.org — 19.28M US undergraduate enrollment, Fall 2024
NCES NPSAS 2019-20 — 72% of undergrads received some financial aid; 55% received federal aid; avg federal aid $8,700
Federal Student Aid / educationdata.org / Statista — ~6.03M Pell recipients AY2022-23; 6.3-6.5M AY2023-24
IIE Open Doors 2024/25 — 357,231 international undergraduates (+4% YoY); 1.18M total international students
MDRC 'Aid Like a Paycheck' RCT (~9,000 students, TX & CA community colleges)
Talker Research / Bango — Gen Z ~$97.70/mo media spend, subscribes to ~26% more services than avg American
Bill-splitting apps market (market.us) — ~$612M in 2025, ~7-8% CAGR; Splitwise 35M+ users
YNAB — free year for college students; $14.99/mo regular price

gaps: No direct, sourced conversion rate of students to PAID budgeting apps — WTP inferred from adjacent spend.
Segment sizes overlap heavily; no de-duplicated sizing exists.
Pell is a proxy for 'lump-sum-refund-dependent'; exact refund population unmeasured.
Upstream '68%/59%' stats passed in without traced primary survey.
No willingness-to-pay figure specific to AI/automation feature set.
nextSteps: user-research-agent: run WTP interviews on ICP; validate 'save-me-money-on-subscriptions' as monetization wedge.
market-research-agent: size de-duplicated SAM/SOM; evaluate B2B2C institutional channel given primary segment's low direct WTP.
Trace upstream '68%/59%' statistics to citable primary survey.
Validate lump-sum-refund population precisely via NPSAS microdata.
Resolve size-vs-monetization tension: highest-severity segment (aid-dependent) has lowest WTP; best WTP is subscription-heavy/cost-sharing segments.
